Know which grant report needs attention next.

A private deadline tracker for small nonprofits managing several awards in spreadsheets. Add your own award dates and reporting intervals, then get a review queue you can export.

After using this, you can now see upcoming and overdue grant reporting work with the remaining restricted balance, which used to take a hand-maintained spreadsheet. See how the review queue is sorted with a worked example, how this compares to GrantHub if you are weighing a paid grant-management subscription, or how it compares to tracking grants in a spreadsheet if you already keep one.

Also tracking pending applications alongside awarded grants, or weighing a grant writer against cash a late report puts at risk? The grant deadline tracker keeps those deadlines next to award balances — nothing uploaded.

Add a grant award

Awards are saved only in this browser so your review queue is still here next time.

Review queue

No awards yet. Add the first one above, or load sample grants to see how the queue reads.

GrantFunderLast filedNext reportStatusRestricted balance

Grant information stays on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

Common questions

How is the next report date calculated?

Award date plus the reporting interval you entered, in months, unless a report has been filed — then it is the last filed date plus the interval instead, so a multi-year award keeps rolling forward rather than staying pinned to its first-ever due date. Set that anchor either by filling in Last report filed when you add the award, or by pressing Filed today on its row in the queue once you have actually sent the report. A 31 January anchor reporting every month lands on 28 February rather than rolling into March, so the interval stays consistent even when it crosses a shorter month.

When does a report count as "Due soon" versus "Overdue"?

Due soon means the next report date is within 30 days of today. Overdue means that date has already passed. Anything further out shows On track. The comparison uses your own device's local date, not a server's clock.

What is the restricted balance?

Award amount minus what you have recorded as spent. It is arithmetic on the two numbers you entered, not a determination of what a funder will allow as an eligible expense.

Do the sample grants use real award data?

No. "Load sample grants" generates three placeholder awards timed relative to today's date so you can see one overdue, one due soon, and one on-track row before entering your own awards. Nothing about them is fetched or saved anywhere.

Is this a substitute for my grant agreement's reporting requirements?

No. The queue is a planning aid built from dates and amounts you supply. It does not read your award agreement, determine allowable costs, or confirm a funder's actual deadline — check the agreement and your grant professional for that.

Where is my grant data stored?

In this browser's local storage only. Nothing is uploaded to a server, and closing the tab does not lose your awards — they are still there next time you open the page on the same device and browser.

vs-granthub.html.text:
← Grant reporting tracker

This tracker vs. GrantHub

GrantHub, from Foundant Technologies, is a well-known paid platform for nonprofit grant work, built to run the whole grant lifecycle for a development team — prospect research notes, proposal drafting and deadlines, a shared document library, and reporting tasks, sold as an ongoing subscription described on foundant.com/products/granthub. It is the kind of tool a grants team reaches for when the job is running an entire program across several staff members.

That is a different job from the one this page does. This tracker has no prospect database, no proposal workflow, and no document library. It exists for the narrower task that starts after an award is already signed: keeping the reporting deadlines and restricted balance on the awards you already hold somewhere you will actually check, with nothing to sign up for.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Where should we look for our next grant, and how do we manage a proposal through drafting and submission? GrantHub or a comparable paid platform — prospect research and proposal workflow are jobs this page does not attempt.
When is the next progress or financial report due on an award we already have? This tracker — enter the award date and reporting interval, get the current due date, and see it flagged overdue or due soon, with no signup.
How much of an award is still unspent, across several awards at once? This tracker — it turns each award's amount and spend into a restricted balance and sorts the whole list by which report needs attention first.
Do we need a shared document library, team assignments, or a record of grant history across a multi-person development team? GrantHub or a comparable paid platform — this page has no accounts, no team features, and remembers nothing about your organization between visits except what your own browser stores locally.

This tracker is deliberately the opposite shape from a subscription platform: nothing to sign up for, nothing billed monthly, and nothing typed here ever leaves your browser. That makes it useful for one small organization that just needs to stop missing a report on the awards it already has, and the wrong tool for a development team building out a formal, multi-person grants program — that is exactly the job a paid platform like GrantHub is built for.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this tracker or a paid platform like GrantHub?

They answer different questions. GrantHub, from Foundant Technologies, is a paid subscription platform built to run a nonprofit's whole grant lifecycle — prospect research notes, proposal tracking, a document library, and team collaboration across a program, described on Foundant's own site. This tracker does none of that. It is a free, browser-only page for a narrower job: once you already hold an award, keeping its reporting deadlines and restricted balance somewhere you will actually check, with no account, no team features, and nothing uploaded. An organization building out a formal, multi-person grants program is looking for the wrong tool here; a coordinator who already has awards and just needs the next report date is in the right place.

Is this page affiliated with Foundant or GrantHub?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Foundant Technologies or GrantHub. GrantHub is named here only to describe what this tracker is and is not.

vs-tracking-grants-in-a-spreadsheet.html.text:
← Grant reporting tracker

This tracker vs. tracking grants in a spreadsheet

A spreadsheet can do exactly what this tracker does -- hold every award's date, reporting interval, amount, and spend, and turn that into a next report date and a restricted balance. Nothing about the underlying math is exotic. What a blank spreadsheet does not give you is calendar-correct month arithmetic built in (a 31 January award with a one-month interval has to land on 28 February, not roll over into March), or an automatic re-sort by urgency every time you open the file, rather than however the rows happened to be ordered when a report was last added.

This tracker is that structure already built: enter an award's date, reporting interval, amount, and spend, and it computes the next due date with the month-length edge cases handled, flags it overdue or due soon against today automatically, and keeps the whole list sorted by which report needs attention first every time the page loads.

QuestionWhere to answer it
Can a spreadsheet track the same award date, interval, amount, and spend? Yes -- the underlying fields are the same either way.
Does a one-month interval off a 31st-of-the-month award date land on the right day? This tracker — DATE() formulas that don't clamp to the shorter month roll over instead of landing on the last day, a mistake that's easy to miss until a report looks a few days late for no reason.
Will the row that just became overdue actually sort to the top? This tracker, automatically. In a spreadsheet, only if you remember to re-sort after every edit.
Do I need to build the formulas myself, or maintain them as awards are added? This tracker: no formulas to write. A spreadsheet: yes, and they need to be copied correctly down every new row.
Do I need a shared file several staff can edit together, or custom columns for my own workflow? A spreadsheet — this tracker has no accounts, no sharing, and a fixed set of fields.

Most of what a spreadsheet gets wrong here isn't the arithmetic, it's the maintenance: a formula that doesn't clamp to a shorter month, or a sort order that goes stale the moment one more award is added. This tracker trades the spreadsheet's flexibility for a page that already gets both of those right, with nothing typed here ever leaving your browser.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Isn't a spreadsheet just as accurate as this tracker?

A carefully built one can be — next report due date is award date plus the reporting interval in months, and restricted balance is award amount minus spend, which is ordinary date and subtraction math. The risk is not that the math is hard, it's month-length edge cases (a report interval that lands on 31 January needs to become 28 February, not 3 March) and remembering to re-sort every row by urgency after each edit across several awards, rather than scrolling past the one that quietly became overdue.

What does this tracker do that a spreadsheet doesn't do automatically?

It computes each award's next report date with calendar-correct month arithmetic, flags a row overdue or due soon against today's date without you checking, and keeps the whole list sorted by which report needs attention first — every time you open the page, not only the moment you last touched the spreadsheet. A spreadsheet does none of that unless you build the formulas and re-sort yourself, and the sort is the step most likely to be skipped when you're only adding one row.

When is a spreadsheet the better choice?

When you need something this tracker doesn't do: a shared file several staff edit together, custom columns for your own workflow, or a permanent record kept somewhere other than your own browser. This tracker stores what you enter only in your browser and is built for the narrower job of not missing the next report on the awards you already hold.

when-is-my-grant-report-due.html.text:
← Grant reporting tracker

When is my grant report actually due?

Managing a handful of awards in a spreadsheet works until two reporting intervals overlap and the one that is actually overdue gets buried under whichever row is at the top. A review queue sorted by days remaining, not by award size or funder name, is what tells you which report needs attention first.

Open the free grant reporting tracker

What a plain award list does not show

The next report date is not the award date. A 6-month reporting interval on an award made in February means the next report is due in August, not on some fixed calendar date someone has to remember separately.

Overdue, due soon, and on track are different problems. Treating every award the same hides the one that already missed its date behind two that still have months to go.

A restricted balance is not a report status. An award can be fully spent and still not be due for a report for months, or barely touched and overdue right now — the two facts move independently.

Worked example

Three awards, reviewed the same day: a $24,000 community program award reporting every 6 months, a $48,000 literacy award reporting every 12 months, and a $15,000 capital award reporting every 3 months.

AwardReporting intervalRestricted balanceStatus
Community food programEvery 6 months$15,500 of $24,000Overdue — 21 days past due
After-school literacyEvery 12 months$16,800 of $48,000Due soon — 14 days out
Winter shelter capitalEvery 3 months$0 of $15,000 (fully spent)On track — 96 days out

Sorted by days remaining rather than award size, the smallest award is the one that needs attention first — the fully-spent capital award is not due for months and would be the wrong place to start. Load the sample grants in the tracker to see this exact queue rendered live.

Common questions

How do I calculate when a grant report is due?

Add the reporting interval in months to the award date, clamped to the last day of a shorter month, to get the next report date. Compare that date to today: a report already past its date is overdue, one due within 30 days is due soon, and anything further out is on track.

What is the restricted balance on a grant award?

It is the award amount minus what has been spent so far. A $15,000 award fully spent has a $0 restricted balance and is not itself a reporting problem — spending is one input to a report, not the trigger for one.

How should I prioritize which grant to report on first when I manage several awards?

Sort by days until the next report, not by award size or funder importance. An overdue report on a small award is a live problem right now; a large award due in three months is not, and treating them as equally urgent means the actually-overdue one gets missed.
